summary: Describes the User-based Security Model for SNMPv3, which provides message-level security such as authentication and privacy for management traffic. It includes a MIB for managing its configuration. It obsoletes RFC 2274 and was replaced by RFC 3414.

plainLanguage.summary: SNMP is how a computer reads and changes settings on routers, switches and other network gear. Earlier versions sent a plain password in every message. This RFC replaces that with a scheme where each message carries a fingerprint that proves who sent it and shows it was not altered, and can optionally be encrypted so that only the intended recipient can read it. It also adds a way to spot a message that is an old copy being replayed.

questions: how does snmpv3 prevent replay attacks
what is the snmpv3 time window
how does snmp key localization work
subtitle: Message-level security for network management: who sent this, was it altered, and is it still fresh.

tldr.problem: Earlier versions of SNMP protected management traffic with a plain community string carried in every message, so anyone who could see the traffic could read it and use it. SNMPv3 needed a model that authenticates messages, hides their contents and detects replays.
tldr.mechanism: The User-based Security Model attaches keys to named users. Each message carries the authoritative engine's identifier, boot count and elapsed time, plus a digest computed over the whole message and, optionally, an encrypted payload. A receiver checks the digest, then checks the boot count and time against a 150-second window.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2574 is a Draft Standard from April 1999 and has been obsoleted by RFC 3414, which restates the same User-based Security Model.

facts.label: Time Window
facts.value: 150 seconds, the same for all users

facts.label: Time to reach that maximum
facts.value: About 68 years at one reboot per second

today: RFC 2574 is a Draft Standard from April 1999, and it has been obsoleted by RFC 3414, which restates the same User-based Security Model for SNMPv3. The RFC itself says it describes the User-based Security Model as used within the SNMP Architecture of RFC 2571, and that the security protocols it defines may be replaced or supplemented later.

sections.title: Why SNMPv3 Needed Message-Level Security
sections.content:
SNMP is how a management station reads and changes settings on network devices. Under SNMPv1 and SNMPv2c the only protection was a community string, a plain word carried in every message, so anyone who could see the traffic could both read it and use it.

This RFC defines the User-based Security Model for SNMPv3. It keeps the familiar idea of a user, identified by a user name, and attaches security information to that user: which authentication protocol to use and its key, which privacy protocol to use and its key, and the operations that change those keys. The model is split into three modules with fixed responsibilities. The authentication module must provide data integrity and data origin authentication. The timeliness module must protect against delay and replay beyond what a normal network causes. The privacy module must protect the payload from disclosure.

The model states plainly what it does not do. It does not try to stop a denial of service, because such an attack is hard to tell apart from an ordinary network failure. It does not address traffic analysis, because management traffic patterns are predictable anyway. And it cannot prove which machine sent a message, only which user the message was sent on behalf of.
sections.plainLanguage: SNMP carries management commands across a network, and older versions had almost no protection. This RFC adds three protections to each message: a check that nobody altered it, a check that it came from an authorized user, and a check that it was generated recently. Encryption is optional on top of that.

sections.title: Users, Keys and Key Localization
sections.content:
Every user in the model has a user name, a security name that is human readable and independent of the security model, and two optional protocols. The authProtocol says whether messages sent for this user can be authenticated and which protocol does it; the privProtocol says the same for encryption. Alongside them are the authKey and privKey, the private secrets those protocols use. The keys are not reachable over SNMP, and a user's key is normally different at each authoritative engine. Two operations, authKeyChange and authOwnKeyChange, and their privacy equivalents, are the only way to update a key remotely, and they are designed so that the update does not need privacy protection of its own.

The key localization algorithm is what lets one password serve many devices. A password is first turned into a key Ku. To get the key for user U at authoritative engine E, the RFC appends E's snmpEngineID to Ku and then appends Ku again, so the engine ID sits between two copies of the key, and runs a secure hash over the result. The output is the localized key. Working backwards from a device's key to the password, or to the key used at another device, is meant to be impractical.

Appendix A gives the password-to-key algorithm, one based on MD5 and one on SHA, and the RFC insists that a password or a non-localized key must never be stored on a managed device. Only the localized key is stored, so that one compromised device does not expose the rest.
sections.plainLanguage: Each account has two secrets: one for proving a message is genuine and one for hiding its contents. The same password would otherwise be needed on every device, so the RFC derives a separate key for each device by mixing the device's own identifier into a hash of the password. Only that derived key is stored on the device.

sections.title: The Security Parameters in an SNMP Message
sections.content:
The security information travels inside the SNMP message in a field called msgSecurityParameters, whose value is the BER serialization of an ASN.1 sequence with six fields. msgAuthoritativeEngineID holds the engine ID of the authoritative engine, msgAuthoritativeEngineBoots and msgAuthoritativeEngineTime hold its boot count and elapsed time, and msgUserName holds the user on whose behalf the message is exchanged. The last two fields, msgAuthenticationParameters and msgPrivacyParameters, belong to the authentication and privacy protocols in use.

These values are what make replay detectable. The authoritative engine keeps its engine ID and boot count in non-volatile storage, and on every restart increments the boot count and resets the time to zero, so the pair of values moves forward without needing a clock that ticks while the device is off. A receiver compares the boot count in the message with its own and the time with its own, and rejects the message if the time differs by more than 150 seconds. A message whose boot count is lower than one the receiver has already seen is an old replay and is rejected.

The engine ID does a second job, defeating the replay of a message captured from one engine to another: the receiver checks that the message names it as the authoritative engine. A zero-length user name matches no user but is allowed, because the discovery procedure uses it.
sections.plainLanguage: Every protected message carries six pieces of information: which device is in charge of the exchange, how many times that device has restarted, how long it has been up, which user the message is for, and the two protocol-specific blocks. The restart count and the uptime are what let a receiver reject an old copy of a message.

sections.title: Securing a Message and Checking an Incoming One
sections.content:
When a message goes out, the engine looks up the user in its local configuration datastore, refuses to send if the requested security level needs a protocol the user does not have, then encrypts the scopedPDU if privacy was requested, fills in the engine ID, boot count, time and user name, and finally computes the digest over the whole message if authentication was requested. The digest is calculated last, so it covers every other field, and the message is then serialized and sent.

When a message arrives, the receiver parses the security parameters, looks up the engine ID and the user, checks that the requested security level is one the user supports, verifies the digest over the whole message, checks the boot count and time against the Time Window, and only then decrypts the payload. Each failure increments a counter in the MIB: unknown engine ID, unknown user name, unsupported security level, wrong digest, outside the time window, or a decryption error.

Discovery comes first. A manager that does not yet know the engine ID sends a request with no authentication and no privacy, a zero-length user name and a zero-length engine ID. The agent answers with a Report PDU carrying its engine ID in the security parameters. If authenticated communication is wanted, the manager then sends an authenticated request with the newly learned engine ID and a boot count and time of zero; the agent's Report carries its current boot count and time, and the manager's local copy is updated as a side effect of processing that message.
sections.plainLanguage: Sending and receiving are mirror images. The sender encrypts the payload if asked, fills in the bookkeeping fields and signs the finished message; the receiver checks the signature before doing anything else, then checks the timing, then decrypts. A first message with no details at all is used to learn the device's identifier before anything protected can be sent.

sections.title: HMAC-MD5-96 and CBC-DES
sections.content:
The RFC defines one authentication protocol that every implementation must support and one it should support, and one privacy protocol. HMAC-MD5-96 computes an HMAC using MD5 over the whole message and sends the first 96 bits, which is 12 octets, of it in the authentication parameters. The key is 16 octets long. HMAC-SHA-96 does the same with SHA instead of MD5.

The privacy protocol is CBC-DES. The scopedPDU is encrypted in cipher block chaining mode in 64-bit blocks, with the data padded to a multiple of eight octets. The DES key is the first eight octets of the 16-octet privacy key, and the last eight octets are a pre-initialization vector. The actual initialization vector is that pre-vector XORed with a salt made of the sender's 32-bit boot count and a 32-bit counter the sender increments for each message, so the same key is never used twice with the same initialization vector. The salt travels in the privacy parameters so the receiver can rebuild the same vector.

The model is written so that these protocols can be replaced. The authentication and privacy modules are separate from the model itself, each defined by a pair of primitives, authenticateOutgoingMsg and authenticateIncomingMsg for authentication and encryptData and decryptData for privacy, so a new protocol can be dropped in later.
sections.plainLanguage: Two concrete algorithms come with the model. Authentication is a keyed hash over the whole message, shortened to 12 bytes. Encryption uses DES in a chain mode, with a fresh starting value for every message so that the same key is never used the same way twice.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security section gives operational advice. An engine must discard responses that do not match an outstanding request, and must use a different message ID for each request inside a 150-second window, so that a duplicated message cannot be mistaken for a fresh one. Time synchronization should use authenticated messages. The RFC notes that SNMP imposes no message ordering, and points at the snmpSetSerialNo managed object for applications that need set operations applied in a defined order.

Secrets should be changed often in proportion to how often they are used, because frequent use gives a cryptanalyst material to work with, and changing a secret after every use is the most secure practice. On users, the RFC says how a user should be defined is a matter of local policy, that people and roles are both possible, and that using the same password for both the authentication key and the privacy key is very poor practice and should be strongly discouraged. It also warns that longer passwords with repeated strings can produce the same key, giving the example that bertbert yields exactly the same key as bertbertbert, and that passwords must be at least eight characters when the appendix algorithm is used.

Finally, the RFC notes that an implementation conforming to the model must implement at least one authentication protocol, keep the user secrets out of reach except for generating and checking messages, implement key localization, and implement the SNMP-USER-BASED-SM-MIB. Implementing a privacy protocol is optional. The MIB objects describe the users and their protocols, so access to them should be tightly controlled.
sections.plainLanguage: The advice is about keeping the machinery honest. Replies that match no outstanding request must be thrown away, request identifiers must not repeat inside the 150-second window, and secrets should be changed often. Using one password for both the checking key and the encryption key is called out as poor practice.

items.label: usmStatsUnsupportedSecLevels
items.desc: Packets dropped because they asked for a security level that was unknown or unavailable.

items.label: usmStatsNotInTimeWindows
items.desc: Packets dropped because they appeared outside of the authoritative engine's window.

items.label: usmStatsUnknownUserNames
items.desc: Packets dropped because they referenced a user the engine did not know.

items.label: usmStatsUnknownEngineIDs
items.desc: Packets dropped because they referenced an snmpEngineID the engine did not know.

items.label: usmStatsWrongDigests
items.desc: Packets dropped because they did not contain the expected digest value.

items.label: usmStatsDecryptionErrors
items.desc: Packets dropped because they could not be decrypted.
